Built to a Standard, Not a Price

Every truck starts as a line-setting ticket — the same document the factory used to specify a build. Ours runs longer.

A Scout II left Fort Wayne with 196 horsepower and drum brakes. We keep the shape and the spirit, and replace everything that made one hard to live with. The result drives like something built this decade and looks like it never left 1974.

Heritage

Why the Scout II

There were four ways to build this truck. We looked hard at all of them and chose the one nobody else was doing properly.

By 1974 the segment was crowded. Ford had the Bronco, Chevrolet the K5 Blazer, Dodge the Ramcharger, Toyota the FJ40. Every one of them is now restomodded by somebody, most of them by several somebodies.

The Scout II is the one that got left behind, and that is precisely the argument for it. International Harvester was a farm-equipment company that built trucks like farm equipment — overbuilt where it mattered, indifferent where it did not. The frame is heavier than a Bronco's. The Dana 44s front and rear were standard, not an option package. The body is flat-sided and honest, without the styling flourishes that date a Blazer to its decade.

What killed the Scout was never the truck. It was a strike, a second oil shock, and a parent company that had to choose between combines and light trucks. Production ended 21 October 1980, ten years before the SUV boom that would have vindicated the whole idea.

What They Got Right
01CHASSIS

The frame is worth keeping

Most restomods start by arguing with the original chassis. We do not. The Scout II frame is a full box-section ladder that was engineered for agricultural abuse, and once it is blasted, repaired and coated it will outlast anything bolted to it. We reinforce the known stress points and leave the rest alone.

The Dana 44s stay too. They were the right axle in 1974 and they remain the right axle now — we rebuild them with 3.73 gears and Warn hubs rather than replacing them with something that would not be an improvement.

02BODY

The proportions are already correct

The Scout II has a short front overhang, a long door, and a bed line that runs straight from cowl to tailgate. Nothing about it needs restyling, which is why our work is almost entirely subtractive — remove the rust, correct the panel gaps the factory never quite achieved, and leave the shape exactly as International drew it.

The grille identifies the year: three horizontal bars through 1972, fourteen vertical bars with chrome for 1973, more chrome in 1974, square headlight bezels from 1975. We keep whatever the truck was born with.

03RANGE

They built the variants we still want

In 1976 the line stretched. The Traveler added eighteen inches of wheelbase and a liftgate; the Terra was the pickup on the same long chassis. The Rallye package ran 1976 to 1980 with its striping and wheels — the specification our own trucks follow, because International had already worked out what the truck should look like at its best.

What We Change

A Scout II left Fort Wayne with 196 horsepower, drum brakes at all four corners on early cars, and a heater that was optional in the first generation. It was built to a price for people who needed a working vehicle, and every compromise in it is a compromise about cost.

Those are the compromises we remove. Not the character — the compromises.

The LS3 goes in because it is the most reliable 430 horsepower available and it fits without butchering the firewall. The 6L80E because a modern six-speed makes the truck usable at highway speed in a way the original three-speed never was. Disc brakes, a Vintage Air system, Dakota Digital gauges, and a wiring loom built new rather than patched — because old-truck electrical is where these vehicles actually fail.

The line setting ticket

Every Scout left Fort Wayne with a build sheet recording exactly how it was specified. On 1977–1980 trucks it was glued inside the glove box door — press the keeper tabs and the box swings down to reveal it.

It is the reason we call our own specification sheets by the same name. When we take a truck to bare frame, the original ticket tells us what it was. Ours records what it becomes.

About

Fifteen years,
three marques

Michael Gisby has spent fifteen years building vehicles people keep. Land Rover Defenders first — one of which sold at Barrett-Jackson for over $430,000 — then K5 Blazers, and now the International Scout II.

The thesis hasn't changed across any of them: take a rugged utility vehicle from an era that built them honestly, and rebuild it so it works the way people actually use trucks now. Keep the shape and the character. Modernize everything underneath.

Huckleberry Harvester is the Scout chapter. Small batch, built in Connecticut, twelve a year.
